title: Next Day
statement:
Give every `Date` object a method `nextDay()`: calling `date.nextDay()` returns the calendar day that follows the object's day, written as a string `YYYY-MM-DD` (a four-digit year, then a two-digit month and a two-digit day, separated by dashes). The method must work on every date object, so it belongs on `Date.prototype`, and it must leave the date it is called on unchanged.

Each case gives `date`, a `YYYY-MM-DD` string. The judge builds `new Date(date)`, which JavaScript reads as midnight **UTC** at the start of that day, and the answer is what `nextDay()` returns for it. Work in UTC (with methods such as `getUTCDate` and `setUTCDate`): the local-time methods depend on the time zone of the computer running the code.
constraints: date is a valid calendar date written as YYYY-MM-DD
notes:
## Intuition

Every date object inherits from `Date.prototype`, so a function stored there becomes a method of all dates, and inside it `this` is the date it was called on. The hard part of "the next day" is the calendar: month lengths, leap years, the end of the year. A `Date` already knows all of that. Setting its day of the month one past the current one makes it roll over into the next month or year on its own, so the method only has to copy the date, add one day, and format the result. (The brute force does the rollover by hand with a table of month lengths and the leap-year rule.)

## Approach

1. Assign a regular `function` to `Date.prototype.nextDay`, so `this` is the date.
2. Copy it into `next` with `new Date(this.getTime())`, leaving `this` unchanged.
3. `next.setUTCDate(next.getUTCDate() + 1)`: day 32 of a month, or day 29 of a non-leap February, rolls over correctly.
4. Read `year`, `month` (the UTC month is 0-based, so add 1) and `day` from `next`, padding month and day to two digits.
5. Join them with dashes.

## Example 1, step by step

`new Date("2014-06-20")` is midnight UTC on 20 June 2014.

- `next` is a copy; `getUTCDate()` is `20`, so `setUTCDate(21)` moves it to 21 June.
- `year` is `2014`, `getUTCMonth()` is `5`, so `month` is `"06"`, and `day` is `"21"`.
- The result is `"2014-06-21"`.

In Example 2, `setUTCDate(32)` on 31 October rolls over to 1 November, giving `"2017-11-01"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1).
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Local-time methods (`getDate`, `setDate`) follow the computer's time zone. In New York, midnight UTC on 20 June is still 19 June, so `getDate()` returns `19`.
- `getUTCMonth()` counts from `0` for January; forgetting the `+ 1` gives the previous month.
- Without `padStart`, 9 January comes out as `2022-1-10` instead of `2022-01-10`.
- Calling `this.setUTCDate(...)` directly changes the caller's date; work on a copy. `next.toISOString().slice(0, 10)` is a shorter way to format the copy.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `this` | the date `nextDay()` was called on |
| `next` | a copy of it, moved one day forward |
| `year` | the UTC year of `next` |
| `month` | the UTC month of `next`, 1-based, as two digits |
| `day` | the UTC day of the month of `next`, as two digits |

narration.1: Store a regular function on Date.prototype, so every date finds nextDay and this is that date.
narration.2: Copy the date, so the one nextDay was called on stays unchanged.
narration.3: Move the copy one day forward; Date rolls over into the next month or year by itself.
narration.4: Read the year of the new day in UTC, the time zone the date string was read in.
narration.5: Months count from 0, so add 1, then pad to two digits.
narration.6: Pad the day of the month to two digits as well.
